# artus-demo-repo

A deliberately small Node project (no dependencies) used to record the
[Artus](https://github.com/demo/artus) demo: a sales-report CLI and a minimal HTTP service.

```bash
npm test                 # node --test
node src/cli.js          # print the report
npm start                # serve it on :3000
```

Some bugs here are intentional — the demo sessions fix and review them.
# Changelog

## 1.1.0
- Add the HTTP service with a `/report` endpoint
- Sort report rows by total, largest first

## 1.0.0
- First release: sales report CLI

content.text: Confirmed the sharpest issue: a client retrying faster than the limit is locked out **indefinitely**, not for one window. Let me load the review submission tool.

input.body:
## Review: per-IP rate limiter

The happy path is correct — I ran the server on an ephemeral port and confirmed exactly 100 requests pass and the 101st gets a `429` with `retry-after`, so the `<= max` boundary is right (allows exactly `max`, no off-by-one).

But the window accounting has a bug that I was able to reproduce, and it turns the limiter into a permanent lockout for well-behaved clients.

### Main issue: rejected requests are recorded, so the window never drains

`recent.push(now)` happens before the limit check, so a blocked request still extends the client's window. Any client that retries faster than `max / windowMs` never recovers. Reproduced with `max=2, windowMs=300` and a client polling every 50ms:

```
polling client: next allowed after >3000 (never) ms (window is 300ms)
quiet client allowed after one idle window: true
```

A client that backs off fully recovers; one that keeps polling (a browser auto-refresh, a retrying mobile client, anything honouring `retry-after` imperfectly) stays blocked forever. This is also the root of a CPU/memory amplification: the per-IP array grows without bound while a client is being blocked, and every request re-`filter`s the whole thing. 5,000 blocked attempts in one window pushed a single `limit()` call to ~50µs, and it keeps climbing — so the harder an attacker is rate-limited, the more work the limiter does per request.

### Also worth fixing

- `hits` is never pruned — one array per distinct IP, retained forever (50k distinct IPs → ~19MB heap). Needs eviction of empty buckets.
- `req.socket.remoteAddress` is the immediate peer, so behind any proxy/LB every user collapses into one bucket and a single client can lock out all traffic. It can also be `undefined`, which I confirmed becomes one shared bucket.
- `retry-after: 60` is hardcoded while `windowMs` is a parameter, so the header lies if the window is ever changed.
- Test coverage only exercises the burst case; the expiry and per-IP-isolation paths — where the bug lives — are untested.

### Unrelated: pre-existing test failures

`npm test` fails 2 tests in `test/dates.test.js` (`parseDay` uses `getFullYear/getMonth/getDate`, which are local-time, against a UTC-documented contract). `src/dates.js` is byte-identical on `main` and untouched here, so this is **not** from this PR — flagging it only so the red suite isn't mistaken for your change. There's already a `fix/date-parsing` branch.

Details inline.

comments.body:
**`hits` is never pruned, so this grows without bound.**

Entries are only ever added or overwritten — nothing deletes a key once an IP goes idle, so the Map retains one array per distinct IP for the process lifetime. 50k distinct IPs measured ~19MB of heap, and the key space is driven by whoever connects (a single IPv6 /64 is effectively unbounded).

Cheapest fix is to drop the bucket when it empties, inside `limit`:

```js
if (recent.length === 0) hits.delete(ip);
else hits.set(ip, recent);
```

That only reclaims IPs that come back one more time after going quiet, so a periodic sweep (or a timestamp-keyed two-bucket scheme) is worth considering if this ever faces real traffic.

`req.socket.remoteAddress` is the immediate TCP peer, not the client.

Two consequences:

1. Behind any reverse proxy, LB, or CDN every request arrives from the same peer address, so all users share one 100-req/min bucket and one noisy client can 429 everyone. If this is only ever exposed directly, fine — but it's worth a comment saying so, since the module comment promises "per client IP".
2. It can be `undefined` (e.g. the socket is already destroyed). `limit(undefined)` doesn't throw, it just buckets every such request under the `undefined` key — I confirmed the second call returns `false` with `max=1`. Rejecting or using a fallback key is clearer than silently sharing a bucket.

Minor, related: IPv4 (`1.2.3.4`) and IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:1.2.3.4`) are distinct keys and each get their own full quota.

`retry-after: 60` is hardcoded while `windowMs` is a configurable parameter of `limit()`. Nothing passes a custom window today, so this is latent rather than broken — but the two will silently disagree the moment someone changes the window. Deriving the value from the limiter (ideally from when the oldest recorded hit expires) keeps the header honest.

Worth noting this header is what nudges clients to retry — and with the line 7 accounting bug in `rateLimiter.js`, a client that retries even slightly early is punished rather than served.

`req.socket.remoteAddress` is the immediate TCP peer, not the client.

Two consequences:

1. Behind any reverse proxy, LB, or CDN every request arrives from the same peer address, so all users share one 100-req/min bucket and one noisy client can 429 everyone. If this is only ever exposed directly, fine — but it's worth a comment saying so, since the module comment promises "per client IP".
2. It can be `undefined` (e.g. the socket is already destroyed). `limit(undefined)` doesn't throw, it just buckets every such request under the `undefined` key — I confirmed the second call returns `false` with `max=1`. Rejecting or using a fallback key is clearer than silently sharing a bucket.

Minor, related: IPv4 (`1.2.3.4`) and IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:1.2.3.4`) are distinct keys and each get their own full quota.

`retry-after: 60` is hardcoded while `windowMs` is a configurable parameter of `limit()`. Nothing passes a custom window today, so this is latent rather than broken — but the two will silently disagree the moment someone changes the window. Deriving the value from the limiter (ideally from when the oldest recorded hit expires) keeps the header honest.

Worth noting this header is what nudges clients to retry — and with the line 7 accounting bug in `rateLimiter.js`, a client that retries even slightly early is punished rather than served.

## Review: per-IP rate limiter

> Submitting as a comment rather than Request Changes (GitHub blocks requesting changes on your own PR) — but treat the first finding as blocking.

The happy path is correct — I ran the server on an ephemeral port and confirmed exactly 100 requests pass and the 101st gets a `429` with `retry-after`, so the `<= max` boundary is right (allows exactly `max`, no off-by-one).

But the window accounting has a bug that I was able to reproduce, and it turns the limiter into a permanent lockout for well-behaved clients.

### Main issue: rejected requests are recorded, so the window never drains

`recent.push(now)` happens before the limit check, so a blocked request still extends the client's window. Any client that retries faster than `max / windowMs` never recovers. Reproduced with `max=2, windowMs=300` and a client polling every 50ms:

```
polling client: next allowed after >3000 (never) ms (window is 300ms)
quiet client allowed after one idle window: true
```

A client that backs off fully recovers; one that keeps polling (a browser auto-refresh, a retrying mobile client, anything honouring `retry-after` imperfectly) stays blocked forever. This is also the root of a CPU/memory amplification: the per-IP array grows without bound while a client is being blocked, and every request re-`filter`s the whole thing. 5,000 blocked attempts in one window pushed a single `limit()` call to ~50µs, and it keeps climbing — so the harder an attacker is rate-limited, the more work the limiter does per request.

### Also worth fixing

- `hits` is never pruned — one array per distinct IP, retained forever (50k distinct IPs → ~19MB heap). Needs eviction of empty buckets.
- `req.socket.remoteAddress` is the immediate peer, so behind any proxy/LB every user collapses into one bucket and a single client can lock out all traffic. It can also be `undefined`, which I confirmed becomes one shared bucket.
- `retry-after: 60` is hardcoded while `windowMs` is a parameter, so the header lies if the window is ever changed.
- Test coverage only exercises the burst case; the expiry and per-IP-isolation paths — where the bug lives — are untested.

### Unrelated: pre-existing test failures

`npm test` fails 2 tests in `test/dates.test.js` (`parseDay` uses `getFullYear/getMonth/getDate`, which are local-time, against a UTC-documented contract). `src/dates.js` is byte-identical on `main` and untouched here, so this is **not** from this PR — flagging it only so the red suite isn't mistaken for your change. There's already a `fix/date-parsing` branch.

Details inline.

Review submitted to PR #1 with 5 inline comments.

**One blocking bug**, reproduced rather than inferred — `src/rateLimiter.js:7` pushes the timestamp *before* the limit check, so rejected requests count against the window. Any client retrying faster than `max / windowMs` refreshes its own window on every attempt and is locked out **indefinitely**, not for one window. With `max=2, windowMs=300` and a 50ms retry loop it was still blocked after 3s (60 windows); a client that goes fully quiet recovers correctly. Same root cause drives a CPU/memory amplification — the per-IP array grows unbounded while blocked and gets re-`filter`ed every request (~50µs/call at 5k entries, still climbing), so limiting an aggressive caller makes the limiter cost more per request.

**Four secondary findings:** `hits` is never pruned (one array per distinct IP forever, ~19MB per 50k IPs); `req.socket.remoteAddress` is the TCP peer, so behind a proxy all users share one bucket, and it can be `undefined` → one shared bucket (confirmed); `retry-after: 60` is hardcoded while `windowMs` is a parameter (latent, nothing sets a custom window yet); tests cover only the burst path, not expiry or per-IP isolation.

The boundary logic is fine — a live server run gave exactly 100×`200` then `429` at #101, no off-by-one.

Two notes on the submission itself:
- `REQUEST_CHANGES` was rejected by GitHub (422 — can't request changes on your own PR), so it posted as `COMMENT`. I flagged the first finding as blocking in the summary body instead.
- `npm test` fails 2 tests in `test/dates.test.js`, but `src/dates.js` is byte-identical on `main` and untouched by this branch — pre-existing, not from this PR (a `fix/date-parsing` branch already exists). I noted it in the summary only so the red suite isn't attributed to this change.
